authored.prompt: Goal: predict deferred execution. `var evens = source.Where(n => n % 2 == 0);` is defined over `List<int> { 1, 2, 3 }`, then `source.Add(4)` runs, then `foreach (var n in evens) Console.Write(n);`. Which observation verifies you understood it?

choices.text: It writes 2 then 4: the filter runs at enumeration time against the list's current contents.
It writes only 2, because Where snapshotted the list when the query was defined.
It writes nothing until ToList() is called on the query.
It throws InvalidOperationException at the foreach: the source list changed after the query was built.

authored.explanation: A deferred query reflects the current state of the source when enumerated, not when defined (10-linq.md:225-231).

authored.prompt: Goal: on C# 14 / .NET 10, get the elements of an `int[] nums` in reverse order WITHOUT modifying the array. Which call does that?

choices.text: Enumerable.Reverse(nums), called explicitly as a static method
nums.Reverse(), which binds to LINQ's lazy Reverse and leaves the array alone
nums.Reverse().ToArray(), forcing the lazy reverse into a fresh copy
Array.Sort(nums) with a descending comparer

authored.explanation: On an array, nums.Reverse() now binds to MemoryExtensions.Reverse(Span<T>) and reverses in place, returning nothing (10-linq.md:208).

authored.prompt: Goal: know what an explicit narrowing cast does with an out-of-range value. `long big = 5_000_000_000L; int overflow = (int)big;` in a default (unchecked) build. Which observation is correct?

choices.text: It compiles and yields 705032704 — only the low 32 bits are kept, with no error.
It throws OverflowException when the cast executes.
It clamps the value to int.MaxValue (2147483647).
It fails to compile with CS0220 because that constant value cannot fit in an int.

authored.explanation: Narrowing casts keep the low 32 bits and are unchecked by default (02-types-and-variables.md:199-200).

authored.prompt: Goal: understand record equality. Two separately constructed `new Person("Sam", "Lee", 30)` values of `public record Person(string FirstName, string LastName, int Age);` are compared with `==`. What does it print, and why?

choices.text: True — records generate value-based equality over all properties.
False — == on any class type compares references.
It does not compile: records need Equals(), not ==.
True only after both instances are first interned with string.Intern.

authored.explanation: p1 == p2 is True: value equality compares all properties (07-structs-records-enums.md:101-102).

authored.prompt: Goal: change one field of a positional record. After `var older = p1 with { Age = 31 };` where p1.Age was 30, which observation verifies how `with` works?

choices.text: older.Age is 31 and p1.Age is still 30: with makes a modified copy.
Both p1.Age and older.Age are 31, since with mutates the original through its init setter.
Compile error: positional properties are init-only, so Age can never be changed.
older and p1 are the same reference, so p1 == older is true.

authored.explanation: Non-destructive copy: the original is unchanged (07-structs-records-enums.md:104-107, 117).

authored.prompt: Goal: declare a small IMMUTABLE positional value-type record (X, Y). Which declaration achieves that?

choices.text: public readonly record struct Pixel(int X, int Y);
public record struct Point(int X, int Y); — positional record structs already get init-only properties
public struct Point { public int X; public int Y; }
public sealed record struct Point(int X, int Y);

authored.explanation: A positional record struct gets ordinary settable properties; add readonly for init-only (07-structs-records-enums.md:142-146).

authored.prompt: Goal: log an exception in a catch block and let it continue up the stack with its ORIGINAL stack trace. Which statement ends the catch block correctly?

choices.text: throw;
throw ex;
throw new Exception(ex.Message);
return; and let the caller check a status flag

authored.explanation: Bare throw; preserves the stack trace; throw ex; resets it (11-exceptions-and-resources.md:108-113).

authored.prompt: Goal: call FetchDataAsync() from code that needs its result without risking the classic async deadlock. Which change verifies the rule?

choices.text: Make the calling method async and write var data = await FetchDataAsync();
Call FetchDataAsync().Result, which waits safely in modern .NET
Call FetchDataAsync().Wait() and then read the task's Result
Call FetchDataAsync().GetAwaiter().GetResult(), which does not block the calling thread

authored.explanation: async all the way down; never .Result/.Wait() (13-async-await.md:142-153).

authored.prompt: Goal: fetch user 1 and user 2 (independent HTTP calls) so the total time is about the slower of the two, not their sum. Which code shape verifies it?

choices.text: Start both tasks without awaiting, then await Task.WhenAll(taskA, taskB).
var a = await GetUserAsync(1); var b = await GetUserAsync(2);
await Task.WhenAny(taskA, taskB) and use only the first result, cancelling the slower call
Run both calls against one shared DbContext inside Parallel.ForEach, concurrently

authored.explanation: Sequential awaits take about the sum; start then WhenAll takes about the slower one (13-async-await.md:81-90).

authored.prompt: Goal: know what the null-forgiving operator does. `string definitely = maybe!;` runs when `maybe` is actually null, and later `definitely.Length` is read. What happens?

choices.text: The ! only silenced the compiler; reading Length throws NullReferenceException at runtime.
The ! adds a runtime null check, so ArgumentNullException is thrown at the assignment.
The ! substitutes an empty string, so Length is 0.
The compiler inserts a null check after the !, which skips the Length read when it is null.

authored.explanation: ! does not change runtime behavior; if you're wrong you still get an NRE (15-nullable-reference-types.md:85).

authored.prompt: Goal: understand what `string?` means once nullable reference types are enabled. Which statement verifies the model?

choices.text: It is compile-time analysis: at runtime string and string? are the same type.
string? compiles to Nullable<string>, a different runtime type like int?.
Assigning null to a non-nullable string throws at runtime once NRT is enabled.
string? turns off null checks for that variable inside the method.

authored.explanation: NRT is a compile-time analysis; the ? signals intent (15-nullable-reference-types.md:17).

authored.prompt: Goal: predict EF Core behaviour. Customers are loaded with `await _db.Customers.ToListAsync()` (no Include, no lazy-loading proxies) and the loop prints `c.Orders.Count` for each. What happens?

choices.text: Every customer prints 0: Orders was never loaded, a silent wrong answer.
One extra query per customer: EF loads Orders on first access, the classic N+1.
EF throws because the navigation was not Included.
EF sees the loop touch Orders and joins them into the first query automatically.

authored.explanation: Lazy loading is off unless proxies are installed; without it c.Orders is empty and prints 0 (19-entity-framework-core.md:204-207).

authored.prompt: Goal: know where an EF Core query stops being SQL. A query puts a custom C# method `MyComplexFormat(c)` inside `.Where(...)` before `ToListAsync()`. What does modern EF Core do?

choices.text: It throws, because a Where it cannot translate is never run on the client.
It silently pulls every row and filters in memory.
It translates the method body into a SQL function automatically on the server.
It ignores the predicate and returns all rows.

authored.explanation: Only the final Select may run on the client; an untranslatable Where/OrderBy always throws (19-entity-framework-core.md:236).

authored.prompt: Goal: make a read-only GET endpoint's EF query faster and lighter on memory. Which change verifies the guidance?

choices.text: Add .AsNoTracking() to the query.
Call SaveChanges() after the query to flush the change tracker.
Add .Include() for every navigation property.
Replace ToListAsync() with a foreach over the DbSet.

authored.explanation: For read-only queries disable tracking: faster, less memory (19-entity-framework-core.md:221-232).
